sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses the connection between the manna from heaven and the Torah, questioning the nature of the test and the superiority of the manna over bread from the earth.

translations.translation: "Behold I will rain down for you bread from the heavens" etc.
(And it explains that this is)
"in order that I may test them, whether they will walk in My Torah or not."
And the precise points of our Nesi'im in this verse are known,
what is the connection between the matter of the manna
(bread from the heavens)
with the matter of the Torah.
And especially that it says "in order that I may test them whether they will be able to receive the Torah,"
meaning that through this test they would know if they will walk in My Torah or not,
for upon this test depends the matter of receiving the Torah.
And also, what is the meaning of the expression "walk in My Torah,"
it should have said, as in other places, an expression of study,
which is appropriate for the Torah, being a matter of intellect,
or "keep My Torah" and the like.
Another point to be clarified,
that since they say on the fifteenth of Iyar
"Behold I will rain down for you bread from the heavens,"
it is understood that this is a novel thing relative to the bread from the earth that they ate until the fifteenth of Iyar,

and seemingly it is not understood, for there is a great superiority in the bread from the earth that they ate then, which was from the matzah cakes that they ate in the land of Egypt, concerning which they were commanded "with matzot and bitter herbs they shall eat it,"
for the matter of matzah is connected with the redemption,
and as explained in the discourses of Pesach,
that the matter of matzah
(although it is a matter of smallness,
nevertheless)
is the smallness of Abba, and as the saying,
"a child does not know how to call 'Abba'... until he tastes the taste of grain,"
for through this there was the revelation that the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed Himself upon them in His glory and His very Self and redeemed them,
from all of which the greatness of the superiority of bread from the earth is understood,
and nevertheless they say that
(this is not sufficient and)
there is a novel thing that is added specifically through the bread from the heavens.
Another point to be clarified,
that the novelty of the bread from the heavens was that it came without the work and toil of man, like bread from the earth,
but rather as it says "Behold I will rain down for you,"
meaning that it came from above,
and if so, it is not understood what is the expression "rain down,"
for the matter of rain is not like the matter of dew, that dew is not withheld,
but rather it is dependent upon the work of man,
and as explained in the discourses of Haazinu,
the difference between "may my teaching drop as the rain, my speech flow as the dew."
